intro: Baarn is a villa village that royalty, bankers and a university all planted for their own reasons, and the trees outlasted every one of those reasons. The Cantonspark spent seven decades as Utrecht University's botanical garden, which is why a dawn redwood and a giant sequoia stand in a free village park. Kasteel Groeneveld's lanes are Staatsbosbeheer ground now, open to anyone. And in the Pekingtuin stands a red oak from around 1850 that the village likes enough to have given its own protective ring. All five are free.
meta_description: Baarn's remarkable trees: a red oak from 1850 the village ringed in honour, exotics from a former university botanical garden, and estate veterans.
question_meta: Baarn's best-documented old tree is the American oak of the Pekingtuin, around 1850. Its story, and four more remarkable trees a walk apart.
question_answer: The best-documented old tree in Baarn is the American oak of the Pekingtuin, planted around 1850, with a trunk of 5.52 metres around. The copper beech by the south pond at Kasteel Groeneveld may be older still, at an estimated 150 to 200 years, but its age is inferred from girth rather than recorded.
question_context: Baarn's trees are the residue of three different ambitions. The Pekingtuin was the garden of a vanished villa named Peking, and its red oak predates the park that formed around it; in October 2021 the municipality placed a protective ring around the trunk and invited villagers to submit inscriptions for it, which is the kind of honour most towns reserve for statues. The Cantonspark explains itself differently: from 1920 to 1987 it was Utrecht University's botanical garden, and when the university left, the exotics stayed, so a village of thirty thousand keeps a dawn redwood and a giant sequoia the way other towns keep a war memorial. Kasteel Groeneveld's tulip tree grove and copper beech belong to the estate-building era, when a good lane of trees was how you showed the neighbours you intended to stay. The ages here are honest rather than uniform: the oak's is well documented, the beech's is an estimate from girth, and each page says which is which.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Baarn?
faq.a: The best-documented is the American oak of the Pekingtuin, planted around 1850, with a 5.52 metre trunk. The copper beech at Kasteel Groeneveld may be older, estimated at 150 to 200 years, but that figure is inferred from girth rather than recorded.

faq.q: Why does a village like Baarn have a sequoia and a dawn redwood?
faq.a: Because the Cantonspark was Utrecht University's botanical garden from 1920 to 1987. When the university withdrew, the collection's trees stayed behind in what is now a free public park, open daily.

faq.q: Are Baarn's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: All five are free. The Pekingtuin and Cantonspark are public parks in the village itself, and Kasteel Groeneveld is a Staatsbosbeheer estate with open grounds. Paleis Soestdijk's park, which holds more old trees, currently opens on a paid and limited basis and is not on this list.

faq.q: What happened to the Kronkelbeuk in the Pekingtuin?
faq.a: The famous twisted beech that generations of Baarn children climbed no longer appears to be standing; it is recorded in our research as gone rather than listed as a tree to visit. If you know more about when and why it disappeared, the suggestion form on every page reaches us.

trees.name: The Cantonspark Dawn Redwood

location.neighbourhood: Cantonspark, former Utrecht University botanical garden

trees.story:
Until 1941 this species existed only as a fossil. Botanists had described Metasequoia from imprints in stone and assumed it had been gone for millions of years, and then a stand of them turned up alive in central China. Seed went out to the world's botanical gardens within a few years, and Baarn got some of it. This tree germinated around 1948, which makes it one of the first generation of dawn redwoods to grow in Europe since the species disappeared from the record entirely.

It has grown fast. It measured 4.22 metres around in 2008 and 5.10 metres by 2021, and over roughly the same decade its height went from 25.4 metres to 28.2. By the standards of its own kind it is still a child.

The park explains the company it keeps. Cantonspark was laid out in 1902 as the private garden of the industrialist August Janssen, taken over by Utrecht University in 1918 as its botanical garden, and handed to the municipality as a free public park in 1987. Seven decades as a teaching collection is why a Dutch village park holds a living fossil, a giant sequoia and a pinetum.

One honest note. The most recent confirmation we could find, measurements and dated photographs, is from October 2021, and the pin marks the park rather than the exact stem.

best_time.label: late October and November, when a conifer 28 metres tall turns rust orange and drops every needle it has

trees.transport: Baarn train station, roughly 15-20 minute walk; local bus to Cantonlaan/Javalaan area stops closer

trees.name: The Cantonspark Giant Sequoia

location.neighbourhood: Cantonspark, former Utrecht University botanical garden / pinetum

trees.story:
The tallest thing in this village park is a Californian. A giant sequoia, 5.20 metres around and roughly 34 metres tall when it was last measured in 2014, standing a fifteen minute walk from Baarn station and a long way from the Sierra Nevada, where the species survives in a scatter of groves and nowhere else in the wild.

Nobody wrote down when it was planted, so the age here is an estimate rather than a record. The park was laid out from 1902 for the industrialist August Janssen, passed to Utrecht University in 1918, and the university added a pinetum, a teaching collection of conifers, for its botany students. A girth of 5.20 metres fits a tree put in the ground somewhere in that window. The park's own description calls it one of the tallest and most monumental trees it has and leaves the date alone as well.

What it has stood through is a university career and the end of one. Utrecht ran the garden until 1987, then let it go, and the municipality took it over and opened it free to anyone. The collection stayed exactly where it was and simply became a park, which is why a sequoia and a dawn redwood now share a lawn with dog walkers.

Two honest notes. The measurements above date from 2014, and the pin marks the park rather than the specimen.
trees.transport: Baarn train station, roughly 15-20 minute walk; local bus to Cantonlaan/Javalaan area stops closer

trees.name: The Tulip Tree Grove at Kasteel Groeneveld

location.address: Near the ijskelder (ice cellar), park of Kasteel Groeneveld, Groeneveld 52, Baarn
location.neighbourhood: Landgoed Groeneveld (Staatsbosbeheer estate), west of the castle

trees.story:
Crowd trees together and they race each other. The tulip trees planted at Groeneveld between 1912 and 1915 went in as a grove rather than as specimens, around sixty of them standing close, and the competition for light drove them to 33 and 34 metres, among the tallest of their species recorded in the Netherlands. Their trunks are modest by comparison, between 2.7 and 3.1 metres around. They spent everything on going up.

The place to stand is the ice cellar. The estate's ijskelder, a brick chamber dug to hold winter ice through the summer, sits at the foot of the three tallest, and it now serves as a hibernation roost for bats. Above it the grove closes over your head.

There is a catch to a tulip tree this tall, and the local nature society states it plainly: the flowers, green and orange and genuinely tulip-shaped, open so high in the crown that most visitors only ever see them after they have fallen. In June, look down.

This entry is a grove, not a single stem, so come for one destination rather than one trunk. The original planting is around 113 years old; smaller trees mixed in among them are later infill, and the pin marks the ice cellar rather than any individual tree.

best_time.label: late October and November, when sixty crowns turn clear yellow at once

trees.access: Free, public Staatsbosbeheer estate park; walkable outside the castle's own opening hours too
trees.transport: Bus from Baarn or Hilversum station to Groeneveld/Amsterdamsestraatweg stop, then short walk; no direct train station on site

trees.name: The Copper Beech by the South Pond, Groeneveld

location.address: Near the southernmost pond, park of Kasteel Groeneveld, Groeneveld 52, Baarn

trees.story:
At 5.28 metres around, this is the thickest beech on the Groeneveld estate, and the number comes with an asterisk. It was measured a metre off the ground rather than at the standard 1.3 metres, almost certainly because something at chest height, a low limb or a spreading buttress, made the usual spot unmeasurable. So it is not directly comparable to the estate's other big beeches, which run from 4.00 to 5.05 metres taken properly. It is still the largest of them by a wide margin.

Nobody recorded when it went in, so the age above is inferred from its girth and from what was happening around it. Groeneveld's grounds were first laid out in Dutch Baroque geometry and then loosened into English landscape style through the nineteenth century, particularly after 1830, and a solitary copper beech placed for effect beside water is exactly that fashion. An open-grown beech this thick is usually put somewhere between 150 and 200 years old, which is a range and not a date.

Most of the estate's beeches stand together in a copse west of the castle, competing and drawn up thin. This one has stood alone by the southernmost pond, which is why it carries the low, wide frame it does, roughly 27 metres tall and spreading. With the leaves down, that frame is the reason to walk out here in January.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are gone and the whole low, wide frame of it shows across the pond

trees.name: The American Oak of the Pekingtuin

location.address: Pekingtuin, on the lawn near the Javalaan side, Baarn
location.neighbourhood: Pekingtuin, village centre, near Baarn railway station

trees.story:
Planted around 1850 and now 5.52 metres around, the American oak of the Pekingtuin is the heaviest trunk in Baarn's village centre, and it stands five minutes from the railway station in a park that costs nothing to enter.

Quercus rubra comes from the eastern United States, and the Dutch call it the Amerikaanse eik. This one went into the ground as an exotic in the private grounds of Villa Peking, decades before the railway and the villa quarter around it took their present shape. What is left of that garden is the park: a wide lawn carrying very large trees, most of them oaks, with a bandstand from 1948 at one end. The Torenlaan that ends at the villa was laid out in the 18th century as a sight line to the tower of the Pauluskerk, so the ground this tree stands on was already being composed as a view a century before anybody planted it.

The park's best known feature belongs to a different tree. About sixty metres west, a smaller one stands inside a corten steel ring carrying a line by the poet Ewoud M. Rosenthal, set into the grass in 2021 to keep feet off the roots. The oak has no ring around it. It is simply the biggest thing on the lawn.

best_time.label: late October and November, when a red oak's leaves turn scarlet
